newsitem.title: USA: United Air parent says earnings rose in quarter.
newsitem.headline: United Air parent says earnings rose in quarter.

text.p: The parent company of United Airlines Tuesday reported a fourth-quarter profit compared with a loss a year earlier, capping its second straight record year and a strong performance for most major airlines.

Two regional carriers reported mixed results. The parent of America West Airlines said earnings rose for the quarter but fell for the year, while Alaska Air reported a loss for the quarter but higher profits for all of 1996.

The results from United came after Delta Air Lines said last week that earnings jumped 79 percent for the latest quarter, Continental reported a 15 percent rise and Northwest Airlines said profits excluding special items rose seven-fold.

UAL Corp., the parent of United, the nation's largest airline, said it earned $20 million, or 12 cents a share, in the quarter, excluding one-time charges, compared with a loss of $18 million, or 58 cents a share, in the 1995 quarter.
Revenues grew 8 percent to $3.98 billion from $3.67 billion.
"United enjoyed its second consecutive year of record earnings while carrying a record 81 million passengers," Chairman Gerald Greenwald said in a statement.

Greenwald said the improved results came despite higher fuel prices and a tax on airline tickets reimposed by the federal government in the quarter. He said United's growth in domestic passenger traffic outstripped the industry average.

For the year, UAL said earnings jumped 59 percent to $600 million, or $6.39 a share, from $378 million, or $4.90 a share, in 1995. Revenues rose 9.5 percent to $16.36 billion from $14.94 billion. Earnings for the latest quarter and year excluded losses from the early retirement of debt.

UAL officials said the company expected 1997 to be another record year, aided by an expected decline in fuel prices, moderate economic growth and controlled capacity growth in the industry. Soaring fuel prices added $350 million in costs during 1996, the airline said.

United's recent labour woes, however, remain a wild card. Earlier this month, United's pilots rejected a wage proposal that offered a 10 percent wage increase over four years. The carrier's mechanics also recently rejected a wage proposal.
The airline and the pilots will now submit their dispute to an arbitrator.
United President John Edwardson said the airline expected its employee-ownership plan to remain successful despite the recent clashes with the labour groups.
"The ESOP has been successful so far and we are counting on continued support of the employees of this company and continued success of the ESOP," Edwardson said in a telephone conference call.
United said it remained willing to address issues regarding the pilots, who helped formulate the plan that gave employees a 55 percent stake in the company in a deal completed in 1994.

Separately, Phoenix, Ariz.-based America West Holdings Corp. said its earnings doubled to $12.1 million, or 27 cents a share, in the quarter, from $6 million, or 13 cents a share, in the 1995 quarter.
Full-year earnings fell 84 percent to $8.5 million from $53.8 million, but the latest results included a one-time charge of $65.1 million. Sales rose 12 percent to $1.74 billion.

Seattle-based Alaska Air Group Inc. reported a loss of $5.6 million, or 38 cents a share, for the quarter, compared with a loss of $800,000, or 6 cents a share, in the 1995 quarter. For the year, it said earnings more than doubled to $38 million, or $2.65 a share, from $17.3 million, or $1.28 a share, in 1995. Sales grew 12 percent to $1.59 billion.
